---
title: "06 — Fast Polynomial Algorithms"
---

A polynomial is a finite coefficient array, but it is useful to think of it as
a compact description of size-indexed choices: $[x^k]A(x)$ is the answer for
total size $k$. This chapter explains why the fast operations work and when
their algebraic preconditions hold. It assumes your library already supplies
tested convolution and basic polynomial operations.

## Prerequisites, notation, and learning objectives

Read [fields and modular units](../01-modular-algebra/chapter.qmd) and
[counting products](../04-combinatorics/chapter.qmd). You should learn to
justify transform multiplication, prove the division/remainder invariant,
recover a polynomial from samples, and recognize correlations and shifts.

Write $A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{a}a_ix^i$, where $x$ is an indeterminate and $a_i$
belong to a commutative coefficient ring $R$. The degree is the largest index
with nonzero coefficient; the zero polynomial has no ordinary finite degree.
We use $\deg0=-\infty$ when comparing degrees. A polynomial equality means
coefficientwise equality; it need not mean equality as functions on a finite
field (for example $x^p-x$ vanishes everywhere in $\mathbb F_p$).

Let $M(n)$ be the arithmetic-operation cost of multiplying polynomials with at
most $n$ coefficients. For FFT-compatible lengths, $M(n)=O(n\log n)$.
Complexity estimates assume $M(n)/n$ is nondecreasing and costs over
doubling sizes sum to $O(M(n))$, as with schoolbook or FFT multiplication.
Field operations have unit cost here; integer bit complexity is a separate cost.

## 1. Multiplication is adding independent sizes

For $C(x)=A(x)B(x)$,

$$c_k=\sum_{i+j=k}a_ib_j. \tag{1}$$

Each summand chooses an $i$-sized object from $A$ and a $(k-i)$-sized object
from $B$. This “split a total” meaning is why convolution occurs in counting,
DP merging, and formal power series.

The transform idea is simple: evaluate polynomials at a specially chosen set of
points. At every point $z$, $(AB)(z)=A(z)B(z)$, so multiplication becomes
pointwise. An FFT uses complex roots of unity; an NTT uses roots of unity in a
finite field. Interpolation returns to coefficient form.

### Why evaluation at roots is invertible and fast

Work over a field containing a primitive $L$th root $w$, with $L$ invertible.
Primitive means $w^L=1$ and $w^d\ne1$ for $1\le d<L$. For an integer $t$,

$$\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}w^{jt}=\begin{cases}L,&L\mid t,\\0,&L\nmid t.\end{cases}$$

In the second case multiplication of the sum by $1-w^t$ telescopes to
$1-w^{Lt}=0$; its multiplier is a nonzero field element and hence invertible.
If $\widehat a_j=A(w^j)$ and $\deg A<L$, this proves

$$\frac1L\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}\widehat a_jw^{-jk}
=\sum_{i=0}^{L-1}a_i\frac1L\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}w^{j(i-k)}=a_k,
\qquad 0\le k<L.$$

Each coefficient survives only its matching frequency sum. To evaluate fast
when $L$ is a power of two, split even and odd coefficient indices:
$A(x)=A_e(x^2)+xA_o(x^2)$. The point squares $w^{2j}$ have only $L/2$
distinct values, and the pair $w^j,w^{j+L/2}$ combines the same two recursive
values with opposite signs. At each stage every coefficient is in exactly one
even or odd child. Thus $T(L)=2T(L/2)+O(L)=O(L\log L)$; inverse evaluation
uses the same recursion with $w^{-1}$ and final scaling by $L^{-1}$.

For example, over $\mathbb F_{17}$, $w=4$ has order four. The values of
$1+2x$ at $1,4,16,13$ are $3,9,16,10$. The inverse formula recovers
coefficients $(1,2,0,0)$. This is exact finite-field arithmetic, unlike FFT
rounding over complex numbers.

### Transform contract

For an NTT of length $L=2^s$ modulo prime $p$, we need $L\mid p-1$ so the
field has a primitive $L$th root of unity. The result length must cover every
possible degree, so $L\ge |A|+|B|-1$. For example,
$998244353=119\cdot2^{23}+1$ supports powers of two through $2^{23}$.

If the answer is modulo an arbitrary $m$, do not pretend one NTT prime computes
it. Convolve under one or more NTT-friendly primes, reconstruct the integer
coefficient by CRT (or use Garner to perform the same reconstruction directly
modulo $m$ when the bounded coefficients are nonnegative), then reduce. Garner
avoids storing a huge reconstructed integer; it does not remove the
reconstruction-range requirement. For signed coefficients, centered CRT must
also determine whether the representative means $c$ or $c-P$, where $P$ is the
product of auxiliary primes; a direct Garner residue needs the corresponding
sign correction modulo $m$. The number
of primes is determined by a proved bound on the *integer* coefficients: for a
signed coefficient of absolute value at most $B$, centered CRT needs a product
of moduli greater than $2B$. Three primes are a convention, not a proof.
Complex FFT instead needs coefficient splitting and a rounding-error bound.

### Worked failure: insufficient padding

For $A=B=1+x$, the true product is $1+2x+x^2$. A length-two transform knows
only values at roots of $x^2=1$, so it recovers $2+2x$: the $x^2$ coefficient
wraps into the constant term. Evaluation multiplies in $R[x]/(x^L-1)$.
Padding until $\deg(AB)<L$ makes this cyclic product equal the desired ordinary
product. Empty arrays should return the zero polynomial before choosing $L$.

## 2. Division: turn the high-degree end into a series inverse

Assume $B\ne0$ and its leading coefficient is a unit. The zero dividend has
quotient and remainder zero; a unit constant divisor has zero remainder.

Given $A=BQ+R$ with $\deg R<\deg B$, ordinary long division removes the
highest remaining term one at a time. Reversal makes those highest terms become
the low-degree terms of a formal power series, where inversion is fast. If
$\deg A<\deg B$, there is nothing to divide: return $Q=0,R=A$.

Let $k=\deg A-\deg B+1$. Define $\operatorname{rev}_k(F)$ by reading from
$F$'s actual leading coefficient downward, retaining $k$ coefficients and
padding with zeros only after its constant term. Then

$$
\operatorname{rev}_k(Q)
\equiv \operatorname{rev}_k(A)\operatorname{rev}_k(B)^{-1}\pmod{x^k}. \tag{2}
$$

Why is this legal? The leading coefficient of $B$ becomes the constant
coefficient of $\operatorname{rev}_k(B)$; it can be inverted precisely when the
leading coefficient is a unit (equivalently nonzero over a field). Terms from $R$ land
beyond the first $k$ reversed coefficients and disappear modulo $x^k$. Reverse
the quotient back, then compute $R=A-BQ$.

For example, $A=x^3+2x+1$ and $B=x+1$ give $k=3$.
Their reversed prefixes are $1+2x^2$ and $1+x$. Modulo $x^3$,
$(1+x)^{-1}=1-x+x^2$, so the reversed quotient is $1-x+3x^2$.
Reversing yields $Q=x^2-x+3$ and $R=-2$. Multiplying $BQ+R$ recovers $A$.
The inverse used here follows from the geometric series; general fast inversion
is derived in [formal power series](../07-formal-power-series/chapter.qmd).

This costs $O(M(n))$ with fast multiplication. Over a general ring it requires
the leading coefficient of $B$ to be a unit. In particular, modulo a composite
number a nonzero leading coefficient might not be invertible, so this division
contract can fail.

## 3. Product trees and multipoint evaluation

To evaluate $f$ at points $x_0,\ldots,x_{m-1}$, build a balanced tree. A leaf
stores $x-x_i$; an internal node stores the product of its children:

$$P_v(x)=\prod_{i\text{ below }v}(x-x_i).$$

At the root, replace $f$ by its remainder modulo $P_{root}$. A polynomial
remainder modulo $x-x_i$ is its value at $x_i$, so recursively passing the
remainder modulo each child reaches $f(x_i)$ at every leaf. This is the same
divide-and-conquer idea as a segment tree: a node stores the polynomial that
vanishes at all points in its interval.

If $\deg f=O(m)$, fast division at each level costs $O(M(m)\log m)$ in the
balanced case. For a higher-degree $f$, first reducing it modulo $P_{root}$
adds the cost of that division. For a small number of points, Horner's rule is
simpler and often faster; use a product tree only when the asymptotic saving
matters.

## 4. Interpolation reverses evaluation

Given $m$ samples, we seek a polynomial of degree less than $m$. This bound
is essential: adding any multiple of $\prod_i(x-x_i)$ preserves all samples.

Now suppose the points $x_i$ are pairwise distinct in the coefficient field and
the desired values $y_i$ are known. Let

$$P(x)=\prod_i(x-x_i).$$

The polynomial $P(x)/(x-x_i)$ vanishes at every $x_j$ except $x_i$. Dividing
it by its value there, $P'(x_i)$, creates a basis polynomial that is $1$ at
$x_i$ and $0$ at every other sample. Therefore

$$f(x)=\sum_i y_i\frac{P(x)}{(x-x_i)P'(x_i)}. \tag{3}$$

This formula is not magic: each summand is responsible for exactly one sample.
Evaluate $P'$ at all points via the product tree, place $w_i=y_i/P'(x_i)$ at
leaves, and merge children as

$$F_v=F_LP_R+F_RP_L.$$

The merge invariant is that $F_v$ is the sum of all leaf terms
$w_i\prod_{j\text{ below }v,j\ne i}(x-x_j)$. Left terms need exactly the
missing right product and vice versa, so no leaf is lost or repeated.

At the root this is (3), in $O(M(n)\log n)$. If points repeat, $P'(x_i)=0$
and this formula is undefined. Repeated samples with identical values can be
deduplicated; contradictory values admit no solution. **Hermite interpolation**
adds derivative data at repeated points and is a different contract.
For distinct points over a field, a nonzero polynomial of degree below $m$
cannot have $m$ roots: division by each root factor would force its degree to
be at least $m$. Thus the formula gives the unique permitted polynomial.
Over a general ring, require every difference $x_i-x_j$ to be a unit.

For values at the $n+1$ consecutive points $0,\ldots,n$, the denominators simplify to
$i!(-1)^{n-i}(n-i)!$. Prefix and suffix products of $(t-j)$ evaluate (3) at one
arbitrary $t$ in $O(n)$. Factorials must be invertible, so normally $n<MOD$.

## 5. Taylor shift: substitute $x+c$ in one convolution

We want the coefficients of $f(x+c)$, not just its value at one point. Expanding
each monomial gives

$$[x^k]f(x+c)=\sum_{i\ge k}a_i\binom ikc^{i-k}. \tag{4}$$

This says degree $i$ contributes to every lower degree $k$. Expand the binomial
coefficient and reverse the $a_i i!$ array; (4) becomes one convolution with
the array $c^j/j!$, followed by division by $k!$. If $n=\deg f$, put
$u_{n-i}=a_i i!$ and $v_j=c^j/j!$. Then

$$\frac{(u*v)_{n-k}}{k!}=
\sum_{i\ge k}a_i\binom ikc^{i-k},$$

so $(u*v)_{n-k}$ is $k!$ times the shifted coefficient of $x^k$; the final
division by $k!$ is essential. For example, if $f(x)=x^2$ and $c=1$, then the
convolution entries at indices $2,1,0$ are $1,2,2$, and division by
$0!,1!,2!$ gives the coefficients $1,2,1$ of $(x+1)^2$.
The reversal lines up $i-k$ as a convolution index. As with binomial transforms,
this needs the factorials through the working degree to be units; it is normally
used over a prime modulus larger than that degree.

The arrays in the shift have indices $0,\ldots,n$. For output index
$0\le k\le n$, only convolution terms with $u_{n-i}$ and $v_{i-k}$,
$k\le i\le n$, enter index $n-k$. For $f=1+3x+2x^2$ and $c=2$,
the shifted polynomial is $15+11x+2x^2$.

## 6. Many factors: keep merge sizes balanced

For $\prod_i A_i(x)$, multiplying factors one after another repeatedly makes a
large polynomial absorb a tiny one. A divide-and-conquer product tree, or a
priority queue that merges the two smallest degrees, keeps products balanced.
For $k$ positive-degree factors of total degree $N$, a product tree balanced
by number of factors has at most $\lceil\log_2 k\rceil$ levels; total degrees
per level are at most $N$. Under the multiplication assumptions above, it
costs $O(M(N)\log(k+1))$. Degree-balanced merging is often faster when sizes
vary widely. Absorb constants separately in $O(k)$ operations and stop
if a factor is zero; arbitrarily many constants still incur input cost.

If the question only asks through degree $D$, truncate after each merge. In a
knapsack-style product such as $\prod_i(1+x^{w_i})$, coefficients above $D$
can never influence lower coefficients later, so retaining them only wastes
time and memory.

## 7. Worked contest translation: all string alignments

Let a binary text have length $n$ and a pattern length $m\le n$. We want the
Hamming distance at every start $0\le s\le n-m$. Define text indicator
$a_i=[\text{text}_i=1]$ and reversed pattern indicator
$b_{m-1-j}=[\text{pattern}_j=1]$. Then

$$[x^{s+m-1}]A(x)B(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}a_{s+j}[\text{pattern}_j=1].$$

This counts aligned pairs of ones: $i+(m-1-j)=s+m-1$ forces $i=s+j$.
If $u_s$ and $v$ count ones in the text window and pattern, mismatches equal
$u_s+v-2[x^{s+m-1}]AB$. Prefix sums give all $u_s$ in linear time and one
convolution gives all correlations. For text 10110 and pattern 110,
the one-one correlations are $(1,1,2)$ and the distances are $(2,2,0)$.
The pattern reversal is justified by the index equation. Complexity is
$O(M(n+m))$ and linear storage; exact convolution needs coefficient range
through at least $m$.

## 8. Failure checklist and reference

- Before an NTT, verify both the required length and the root-of-unity condition.
- Before a polynomial inverse, verify a nonzero/invertible constant term; before
  division, verify the leading coefficient condition instead.
- Normalize negative coefficients in the target ring.
- For CRT convolution, prove the reconstruction range covers a coefficient.
- Interpolation requires distinct sample points; consecutive-point formulas
  additionally need nonzero factorial denominators.
- Check a small product, quotient/remainder identity, and interpolation samples
  independently of the fast routine.

| Operation | Cost | Contract |
|---|---|---|
| Multiplication | $M(n)$ | Padded length and exact arithmetic/rounding |
| Division | $O(M(n))$ | Nonzero divisor with unit leading coefficient |
| Multipoint evaluation | $O(M(n)\log n)$ for comparable degree and sample count | Monic product-tree divisors |
| Interpolation | $O(M(n)\log n)$ | Degree < sample count; unit point differences |
| One consecutive-point query | $O(n)$ | Distinct nodes 0,…,n; unit factorials |
| Taylor shift | $O(M(n))$ | Unit factorials through the degree |

The [solved exercise sequence](exercises.qmd) checks these contracts through
modelling and counterexamples.
